channel.title: DFIR Radar
channel.description: Keeping DFIR Intelligence on your Radar. The latest DFIR research from hundreds of sources, ranked by relevance for practitioners.

item.title: Frostbitten in France: A Danfoss StoreView Internet Exposure Report
item.description:
Attackers hit hundreds of French 🇫🇷 supermarkets on October 11, pushing Danfoss AK-SM 800A refrigeration controllers into defrost mode, spoiling food and causing fires. Three chained CVEs in internet-exposed management interfaces were the enabling conditions.
- The vulnerability chain starts with CVE-2025-41450 (disclosed March 2025, fixed in firmware 4.2), which let an unauthenticated actor compute a valid admin password from the current calendar date with no credentials. CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452 (disclosed August 2025, fixed in 4.3.1) added authenticated command execution and interface disruption. In August 2026, Claroty demonstrated chaining CVE-2025-41450 with CVE-2025-41451 to reach remote code execution. That proof-of-concept preceded this attack by roughly two months.
- Censys identified 1,825 StoreView hosts in France 🇫🇷 on October 11. Of those, 1,158 ran firmware below 4.2, meaning the date-derived admin password was still valid. By October 14, that count had dropped to 537, a 71% fall. The key finding: patched and unpatched hosts disappeared at the same rate (roughly 70% each), meaning operators pulled devices off the internet rather than patching. The worldwide picture is worse: the three largest globally exposed version groups are 3.3.0 (560 hosts), 4.3.1 (511), and 3.2.6 (437). Ten of the twelve most-exposed countries have more than 60% of their hosts below 4.3.1, led by Poland 🇵🇱 at 81% and Romania 🇷🇴 at 80%.
- The Censys report details a fingerprinting method that responders can replicate: the login-page version string does not match the actual firmware. The real version maps to the Last-Modified HTTP header of html/index.html inside the firmware package. The report extracted timestamps from all 18 public .spk update files available at sm800a.danfoss[.]com/sw_shared/, correlating each to a UTC build date, and matched those dates to Censys scan data. The SHA-256 of the 4.3.1 update is 5a19ee33d9d9fa26302bbf2b1875475c9e97979528fd382e87de39a645b96af2.
- CERT-FR issued emergency alert CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 calling for immediate internet disconnection. The incident echoes a confirmed August 2026 event where US 🇺🇸 Department of Defense commissary freezers went into defrost mode, though no vendor or CVE was ever confirmed for that incident. The pattern is consistent: internet-exposed OT with no network segmentation, running end-of-life firmware that cannot be patched because replacement is cost-prohibitive.
For responders and OT defenders: use the Censys query "host[.]services.endpoints.http.html_title = 'Danfoss StoreView'" to find exposed instances in your environment or on your client's ASM scope. Check the HTTP Last-Modified header against the build date table in the report to determine true firmware version, not the login-page string. If the build date predates July 31, 2025 (the 4.3.1 build timestamp), the device is vulnerable to at least CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452; predating March 4, 2025 means all three CVEs are open. The right remediation is network isolation, not patching alone.

item.title: Determined Attacker Uploads Malicious Webshells to Parks and Rec Management Platform Servers
item.description:
A determined attacker hit multiple tenants of a recreation management platform across four acts, registering member accounts to upload .aspx webshells, hunting cardholder data, and ultimately trojanizing a jQuery file to harvest credentials from every visitor to the login page.
Key findings:
- Initial access came not from the six hours of failed brute-forcing, IIS 8.3 tilde enumeration, WebDAV method abuse, or upload-handler parser bypasses, but from simply registering a legitimate member account and abusing the upload function to drop .aspx webshells into /documents/MemberFiles/. Fourteen files were uploaded on Server 1, using the platform's own naming convention (accountID_memberID_UUID.aspx). The webshell keys wf9x (Act 1) and m7Qx2pL9 (Acts 2-4) identify which shell was in use. The attacker's user-agent Mozilla/5.0+(Windows+NT;+Windows+NT+10.0;+zh-CN)+WindowsPowerShell/5.1.22621.1037 places the locale as Simplified Chinese 🇨🇳.
- Post-access enumeration was systematic and payment-focused. After running whoami, hostname, ipconfig, netstat, and appcmd.exe to map the IIS environment, the attacker parsed web.config files as XML via PowerShell to extract SQL credentials, then used sqlcmd to connect directly to the database hunting for cardholder data. They also ran findstr across Fortis webhook log files at E:\Content\info_fortis\Webhooks\ looking for exp_date, cvv, card_number, first_six, and last_four fields, and searched for AuthorizeNet, Fortis, CardConnect, BluePay, and Stripe references across the content directory.
- The attacker adapted across all three servers, getting quieter each time. On Server 3 they copied webshells disguised as css_bundle.aspx, jquery.validate.min.aspx, and webresource.aspx into IIS include and virtual directory paths, then timestomped those files by inheriting timestamps from E:\Websites\REDACTED[.]com\http\web.config, making them blend into the legitimate file timeline. When defenders cleaned but did not fully lock the third server, the attacker returned using the same registered account and escalated to supply-chain-style payload injection.
- Act 4 was the most damaging attempt. The attacker dropped Base64-encoded files into C:\Windows\Temp (plant_ccrtc_mousewheel.ps1.b64, plant_ccrtc_fast.ps1.b64, ccrtc_sdk_init.js.b64), decoded them to .ps1 and .js, then used the PS1 scripts to locate and append an obfuscated payload into the legitimate jQuery asset jquery.mousewheel-3.0.6.pack.js loaded by /auth/default.aspx. The injected JavaScript pulled a second-stage payload from hxxps://chat.ririmochii.workers[.]dev/core[.]js and established WebRTC and WebSocket C2 channels to hxxps://fk.bubuneeko.workers[.]dev/_cf/rel, hxxps://fk.bubuneeko.workers[.]dev/_cf/ice, and wss://fk.bubuneeko.workers[.]dev/_cf/soc to harvest credentials from every visiting browser in real time. An idempotency guard (function _0x9d66) prevented duplicate payload writes. The PS1 scripts contain comments consistent with AI-generated code, including literal instruction fragments such as "Fast plant: candidate paths only, no drive recurse."
Takeaway: On any IIS-hosted multi-tenant platform, start your hunt in the member file upload directories. Look for .aspx files matching a member account naming pattern in paths like /documents/MemberFiles/. Pull IIS logs and cross-reference w3wp.exe spawning cmd.exe or powershell.exe as a child process. Check C:\Windows\Temp for .b64 files decoded to .ps1 or .js. Audit jQuery and other shared JS assets for appended content and compare file hashes against known-good versions. Examine file timestamps for outliers where creation, modified, and accessed times are identical to nearby legitimate files, a strong indicator of timestomping. The full IOC table, including six SHA256 hashes and the C2 domains, is in the Huntress report.

item.title: Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver: The Trust Gap Attackers Operate Inside
item.description:
BYOVD attacks exploit a structural trust gap, not just a blocklist gap. Revoked certificates still load kernel drivers in 2026, and roughly 36% of catalogued vulnerable drivers remain absent from Windows default block rules.
Key findings:
- The kernel's signing policy accepts end-entity certificates issued before July 29, 2015 if they chain to a cross-signed authority, and Windows loads drivers signed with revoked certificates even when a local revocation list is present. A 2026 intrusion traced by Help Net Security used a decade-old forensic driver whose certificate had expired and been revoked years prior. The kernel loaded it anyway. Attackers also manufacture fresh trust by forging signature timestamps to appear pre-cutoff, turning a dead certificate into a working signing key without breaking the trust chain.
- The LOLDrivers catalog pull dated June 19, 2026 puts 782 of 2,190 samples (36%) absent from the default Windows block rules. Roughly 479 samples (22%) load even with HVCI enabled. The default blocklist updates roughly once or twice a year, the minimum disclosure-to-block window has historically run six months or more, and a frozen Windows 10 blocklist documented in public reporting sat at a December 2019 version until an October 2022 fix, a three-year gap between stated cadence and on-device reality. Dell's dbutil_2_3.sys was disclosed in 2021 and was still disabling security tooling in 2024.
- The behavioral chain is observable end to end without prior knowledge of the specific driver. A service is created via sc.exe (Sysmon Event ID 1, System Event ID 7045), a driver loads (Sysmon Event ID 6), and a device control call drives termination against protected processes. Recent EDR killers also unregister kernel callbacks as a distinct step before process termination. The driver name changes every campaign; the structure does not. Detection keyed to that shape survives a recompile. Detection keyed to a hash does not.
- A Windows security update in April 2026 removes default trust for cross-signed kernel drivers, targeting the timestamp-forgery loophole directly. It does not retroactively address the 36% already off the blocklist. The ASR rule that blocks vulnerable signed drivers only stops a write to disk, not a driver already present from loading, and a driver the policy would block keeps running until the next reboot.
Practitioner takeaway: Instrument Sysmon Event ID 6 for every driver load and flag any signature status that is not Valid (untrusted root, explicit distrust, bad or invalid signatures) and any driver whose hash, signer, or version is first-seen on that host. Neither check requires the driver to be catalogued. Pair with CodeIntegrity Operational log Event IDs 3077 (blocked load), 3076 (audited load), 3089 (signature detail), and 3099 (policy loaded) to prove your blocklist policy actually applied rather than assuming it. The report names Splunk detection content keyed on Sysmon Event ID 6 and notes it requires triage rather than blind firing. IOCs and open tooling referenced include Trail of Bits' HVCI-loldrivers-check and the community loldrivers-database checker to reproduce the coverage measurement against your own fleet.

item.title: The hidden network: Inside the phishing infrastructure ecosystem powering global cybercrime
item.description:
A Chinese-speaking phishing-as-a-service ecosystem sent over one billion phishing emails to 75,000+ orgs since January 2026, with Microsoft's DCU now facilitating a disruption of its core developers and infrastructure.
Key findings:
- Storm-3119 operates YAM Store, an initial access broker that hijacks Microsoft 365 and Azure for Education tenants through a five-stage pipeline: automated Flask/Tor-based reconnaissance, app-only admin panel takeover using stolen client secrets, SharePoint/OneDrive abuse via self-provisioned PnP Management Shell service principals, centralized Cloudflare-based phishing DNS management, and resale through an automated storefront accepting Alipay, WeChat Pay, and USDT (TRC20). Because access is application-level rather than session-tied, the persistence is durable and harder to detect than a standard compromised user account. Storm-3119 also fabricated a fake nonprofit entity named "Jewish Choice" tied to jewishchoice[.]org to create seemingly legitimate tenants.
- Storm-2990 covers three phishing kits sold through YAM Store: CoGUI (also known as NX or FA), Haozi (also known as Phoenix), and Iron Man System, all assessed with high confidence as developed by Chinese-speaking actors. Iron Man System alone contains over 2,335 templates targeting 139 countries, built on the GoFrame open-source Go framework, and hosted predominantly on China-based infrastructure. Kits use geofencing, fake CAPTCHA gates, IP allow/block lists, and Telegram bot exfiltration, including real-time WebSocket credential harvesting with live operator interaction per victim session.
- Downstream activity from Storm-2990 customers includes credential theft via brand-impersonation lure pages, device code phishing to harvest OAuth tokens without a password, and financial fraud using stolen payment data for high-end goods purchases. Targeted sectors include healthcare, financial services, wholesale distribution, and IT across Japan 🇯🇵, the United States 🇺🇸, Australia 🇦🇺, and India 🇮🇳. Lures impersonate toll and traffic authorities, law enforcement, postal services, financial providers, and retail brands in local languages.
- The supply chain here is the story: YAM Store is not just selling phishing kits, it is provisioning the cloud infrastructure those kits run on. The Microsoft report describes Storm-3119 granting itself AppCatalog.ReadWrite.All and broad Microsoft Graph permissions through a compromised Global Administrator account, then converting hijacked SharePoint and OneDrive storage into a sellable hosting product for phishing operators downstream.
Practitioner takeaway: In a Microsoft 365 tenant compromise investigation, look beyond user accounts. Hunt for anomalous service principal creation, unexpected grants of Microsoft Graph permissions (especially AppCatalog.ReadWrite.All and SharePoint API full control), and PnP Management Shell registrations that do not match your environment's baseline. Silent password resets without a forced change at next sign-in and unexplained education license assignments on non-education tenants are specific signals the report ties to Storm-3119 staging. For phishing triage, the Microsoft Entra ID Protection alerts named in the report ("Unfamiliar sign-in properties", "Atypical travel") and Defender for Office 365 alerts for post-delivery URL removal are the detection surface to baseline against this campaign.

item.title: CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134 | AhsayCBS Authentication Bypass and Remote Code Execution Vulnerabilities
item.description:
AhsayCBS backup servers are under active exploitation via a chained auth bypass and path traversal RCE. JSP webshells and XMRig miners confirmed in the wild. CVSS scores of 7.3 and 10.0 (Critical).
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-105133 (CVSS 7.3, High) is an authentication bypass in the JSON API handler. The checkSysPwd() password check is skipped entirely when the request body includes "FromServlet":"Y", making every JSON API action reachable without credentials. This is the entry point for the full attack chain.
- CVE-2026-105134 (CVSS 10.0, Critical) is a path traversal in the replicated-file upload endpoint PUT /rps/obs7/rpsfile/upload. The service builds the destination path from attacker-controlled UserHome and TopDir request headers via getReplicatedPath() without applying the product's own path denylist. Chained with the auth bypass, an attacker writes a JSP file into a Tomcat web-served directory and triggers execution as the AhsayCBS service account. This path requires the target to be configured as a replication receiver.
- Huntress confirmed exploitation beginning October 7, 2026, three days after CVE publication. Observed post-exploitation includes JSP webshells planted under %CBS%\webapps, an XMRig miner dropped as edge.exe in a Temp directory, msedge.exe in a Temp directory (a modified NSSM utility used for persistence), and Taskgmr.ps1 used to conceal mining activity. Mining pool connections were observed to xmr.kryptex[.]network on port 8029. Payload hosting was traced to imagefiles-backup.oss-ap-southeast-7.aliyuncs[.]com.
- Earlier hotfixes v9.15.2.59 and v10.3.4.0 did not fully address these vulnerabilities. The required builds are v10.3.4.45 for v10 deployments and v9.15.2.70 for v9. V7 and v8 customers must upgrade to v9.15.0.0 first, then apply v9.15.2.70. Huntress independently verified that v10.3.4.45 blocks the authentication bypass. A server reboot is required after applying the hotfix.
- Patching does not remove existing webshells, unauthorized accounts, or attacker persistence. Ahsay's own recovery guidance for confirmed compromises is full OS reinstall, fresh AhsayCBS install with the applicable hotfix, and restore from a pre-compromise server configuration. Compromise of the AhsayCBS host exposes centrally managed backup policies, storage targets, and user accounts across the entire environment.
If AhsayCBS is in your environment, treat this as active incident response, not patch management. Start by hunting %CBS%\webapps for unexpected JSP files, reviewing replication receiver configuration for unauthorized additions, and auditing AhsayCBS administrator accounts for accounts you did not create. Check Temp directories for edge.exe and msedge.exe and look for outbound connections to xmr.kryptex[.]network:8029. Restrict management interface access to trusted IPs or behind VPN while remediation is in progress. IOCs are listed in the report.

This path requires the target to be configured as a replication receiver.

- Huntress confirmed exploitation beginning October 7, 2026, three days after CVE publication. Observed post-exploitation includes JSP webshells planted under %CBS%\webapps, an XMRig miner dropped as edge.exe in a Temp directory, msedge.exe in a Temp directory (a modified NSSM utility used for persistence), and Taskgmr.ps1 used to conceal mining activity. Mining pool connections were observed to xmr.kryptex[.]network on port 8029. Payload hosting was traced to imagefiles-backup.oss-ap-southeast-7.aliyuncs[.]com.

- Earlier hotfixes v9.15.2.59 and v10.3.4.0 did not fully address these vulnerabilities. The required builds are v10.3.4.45 for v10 deployments and v9.15.2.70 for v9. V7 and v8 customers must upgrade to v9.15.0.0 first, then apply v9.15.2.70. Huntress independently verified that v10.3.4.45 blocks the authentication bypass. A server reboot is required after applying the hotfix.

- Patching does not remove existing webshells, unauthorized accounts, or attacker persistence. Ahsay's own recovery guidance for confirmed compromises is full OS reinstall, fresh AhsayCBS install with the applicable hotfix, and restore from a pre-compromise server configuration. Compromise of the AhsayCBS host exposes centrally managed backup policies, storage targets, and user accounts across the entire environment.

If AhsayCBS is in your environment, treat this as active incident response, not patch management. Start by hunting %CBS%\webapps for unexpected JSP files, reviewing replication receiver configuration for unauthorized additions, and auditing AhsayCBS administrator accounts for accounts you did not create. Check Temp directories for edge.exe and msedge.exe and look for outbound connections to xmr.kryptex[.]network:8029. Restrict management interface access to trusted IPs or behind VPN while remediation is in progress. IOCs are listed in the report.

item.title: Submit and Execute: Weaponizing Reflected XSS in Siemens Teamcenter's Login Redirect (CVE-2026-58113)
item.description:
CVE-2026-58113, CVSS 8.5 (High), is a zero-interaction reflected XSS in Siemens Teamcenter's /auth/ login-redirect flow. An attacker with no account of their own can silently reassign who can approve engineering releases by sending a single link to an authenticated user.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-58113 lives in the /auth/ endpoint used during Teamcenter Active Workspace SSO. The server reflects arbitrary query parameters and parameter names directly into the attributes of a hidden HTML form without encoding them. Because the page immediately calls document.getElementById('autoSubmit').submit() via a body onLoad handler, the injected attribute fires the moment the page loads. No hover, no click, no second action. The payload structure closes the form's action attribute early with a URL-encoded double quote (%22), injects an onformdata handler as a new form attribute, and re-opens the trailing quote to keep the markup valid.
- The onformdata event is the critical piece. It fires during the browser's entry-list construction phase of form submission, including when submission is triggered programmatically by form.submit(). That makes it a reliable zero-interaction sink in this context, one that is under-represented in standard XSS payload sets and many WAF signatures. Bishop Fox confirmed execution in Firefox and notes behavior may vary across browser engines.
- The weaponized payload went further than a proof-of-concept dialog. The injected handler called Teamcenter's /tc/RestServices/Workflow-2014-06-Workflow/setSurrogate REST API via a fetch request with credentials: include, carrying the victim's session cookies. Teamcenter uses a double-submit CSRF token pattern, which requires the token to be JavaScript-readable from document.cookie, so the injected script simply read it and echoed it in the X-Xsrf-Token header, bypassing CSRF protection entirely. keepalive: true ensured the POST completed even as the page navigated away to the SSO destination. The test confirmed a second account was silently added as a surrogate delegate with a delegation window of roughly one year.
- Surrogate delegation in a PLM system is not a minor setting. A surrogate can approve engineering change orders, release controlled design data, and modify bills of materials, the actions that move physical hardware into production. Beyond surrogate abuse, any Teamcenter API the victim is authorized to call is reachable from the injected script: data exfiltration, record tampering, and privilege escalation are all constrained only by server-side authorization. Every authenticated user is a viable target, making phishing a natural delivery vector. Siemens SSA-157465 covers four affected branches: V2412 fixed in V2412.0013, V2506 fixed in V2506.0010, V2512 fixed in V2512.2607, and V2606 fixed in V2606.2607.
Practitioner takeaway: patch first using SSA-157465, then run a surrogate delegation audit before you close the ticket. Pull active and historical delegation records, flag any assignments users did not initiate, and correlate creation timestamps against authentication-redirect activity and account logins from the same window. For detection without running the payload, inspect reverse proxy, WAF, or application logs for requests to /auth/ containing %22 adjacent to HTML attribute-style text, event handler names including onformdata, onfocus, onerror, or onload in query values, or unexpected arbitrary parameter names on that endpoint. A hit is a lead to investigate the associated session and account, not a confirmed compromise. The report's own detection guidance is the place to start building those signatures.

item.title: Unit 42 Uncovers PEERSTITCH, a Stealthy FortiGate Implant
item.description:
Nation-state-level actors exploited CVE-2024-47575 against a telecom managed service provider's FortiManager, then deployed PEERSTITCH, a novel memory-resident ARM64 implant that leaves no binary on disk, opens no ports, and hides inside legitimate FortiOS daemon memory.
Key findings:
- Initial access via CVE-2024-47575 (FortiJump), which allows unauthenticated RCE through crafted requests to the FMG-Access management channel on TCP port 541. The attackers registered a rogue virtual FortiGate named localhost (serial FMG-VMTM23017412) from 45.32.41[.]202, then exfiltrated a configuration archive containing running configs, SQLite databases (global.db and revinfo.db), serial numbers and public IP addresses for more than 500 managed FortiGate firewalls, and ciphertext credentials that were confirmed recoverable via brute force. The scope extended beyond the provider: those firewalls protected client networks the provider managed.
- Privilege escalation via CVE-2025-61624, a path traversal in the FortiOS CLI auto-script engine. The auto-script object name field accepts traversal sequences without sanitization, so an authenticated super_admin can write arbitrary files as root outside the intended directory. The attackers used the object name ../../../../setup to drop the PEERSTITCH loader, escaping the restricted FortiOS management shell and gaining root on the underlying OS.
- PEERSTITCH (lldprx, SHA-256 b9fb0b27ddd59b58d3ae53c7227298a3e0de1e6f868b9429ae21533bb9cd1e70) is a 64-bit ARM64 ELF injector that uses ptrace(PTRACE_SEIZE) to attach to /bin/miglogd and /bin/iked, allocates a 16 KB RWX anonymous mmap region in each, and writes a 1,344-byte hook payload. The hook uses strstr() to watch for traffic patterns containing TCP port marker 8550 and IP marker 169.254.0.1, extracts session tokens into a 16-slot ring buffer at offset +0x0F0, and forwards them cross-process via open/lseek/write on /proc/counterpart_pid/mem. Three NOP patches (0xAA0003E0, MOV X0, X0) are written to base+0x106F7B8, base+0x1072E20, and base+0x109A570 to suppress tamper detection. No persistent file, no listening socket, no outbound connection. Staged from hxxp[:]//23.240.77[.]233:8085/ and hxxp[:]//47.18.167[.]159:8085/.
- Parallel C2 via Apache mod_md ACME abuse: the attackers pushed a path-traversal auto-script to write ../../tmp/apache2/conf/md-acme.conf, mapping the MDChallengeDns01 handler to /bin/node. Apache's continuous MDRenewMode always polling loop re-executed a reverse shell (SSH to kali@23.240.77[.]233:8084) on every certificate renewal cycle. Anti-forensics were systematic: killall -9 miglogd and killall -9 syslogd before script execution, diagnose debug crashlog clear to wipe Signal 11 crash evidence, automatic rollback of rogue accounts and auto-script objects, lldprx self-unlinking from disk, and overwriting md-acme.conf with the decoy string "#0 certs managed by ACME".
- The attackers also impersonated the FortiManager platform over TCP port 541 using exfiltrated FGFM trust material, pulling full configs from managed firewalls under a fabricated account named FortiGateCloud. Packet capture rules were pushed to downstream firewalls targeting RADIUS (UDP 1812/1813), LDAP (TCP 389), TFTP (UDP 69), and a range of telecom services on TCP ports 3696-3706 to intercept credentials and enumerate topology. CVE-2024-26009 and CVE-2024-26008 are assessed with medium confidence as facilitating FGFM session manipulation.
Practitioner takeaway: Detection requires hunting volatile memory, not disk. On any potentially affected FortiGate, inspect /proc/miglogd/maps and /proc/iked/maps for anonymous rwxp regions of exactly 16,384 bytes. Audit syscall telemetry for cross-PID write() calls into /proc/pid/mem between those two daemons. Run diagnose debug crashlog read and look for Signal 11 crashes involving miglogd, iked, or syslogd, the attackers cleared these but the clearing action itself is a detection signal. Check all FortiOS system.auto-script objects for names containing ../ traversal strings. Treat the exfiltrated FGFM trust material as compromised for every enrolled downstream device: rotate certificates and credentials before trusting restored management connectivity. The Unit 42 report includes a YARA rule (u42_apt_linux_PEERSTITCH_fortigate_implant), eight SHA-256 hashes, and a full network IOC table.

item.title: You don’t need a nation state to warm up a fridge
item.description:
Hundreds of French 🇫🇷 supermarket refrigeration systems were sabotaged overnight on October 11, 2026, spoiling stock across major chains and triggering fires. CVE-2025-41450 in Danfoss AK-SM controllers is at the center of it.
Key details:
- The Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC system managers affected here sit at the top of a store's refrigeration hierarchy, pushing settings down to every case controller and managing alarms. The authentication bypass, CVE-2025-41450, is reached via undocumented attributes in a request to xml.cgi with no valid account required. It returns an admin session if the attacker supplies a code generated from the device's current date by a fixed algorithm with no per-device secret. The controller hands out its own date unauthenticated, so an attacker does not even need to guess. Synacktiv documented a version of this in 2023; Claroty's Team82 published the AK-SM 800A variant in 2026. The algorithm has not been published openly, but firmware reverse engineering to recover it is described as a modest job, after which the same daily code opens every exposed unit and can be scripted. Danfoss patched it in firmware release 4.2. The stores that burned were still running older firmware.
- The damage required more than access. To push a freezer to 50C, an attacker had to force the defrost heaters to stay on and defeat the termination sensor and timer that normally end the defrost cycle. Those parameters, defrost method, schedule, termination temperature, and time limit, are documented in Danfoss manuals. Because the heaters live on individual case controllers rather than the system manager, the attacker reconfigured dozens of controllers, not one, but the system manager is built to push settings to all of them simultaneously. Alarms were disabled at the same time, so no one was paged overnight. The fires appear to be a side effect of running heaters far outside their rated duty cycle, most likely at sites with pre-existing electrical weaknesses.
- These controllers reached the internet through a common operational pattern: refrigeration contractors fit a cellular modem on the unit for remote access rather than going through the retailer's managed network. The retailer often does not own that link, cannot see it, and has no record of it. Standard network security reviews never reach it. Intermarché, Netto, U cooperative, Carrefour Market, Monoprix, and E[.]Leclerc are among the chains named. Spain 🇪🇸, Portugal 🇵🇹, Poland 🇵🇱, Germany 🇩🇪, and Belgium 🇧🇪 have similar reports. CERT-FR issued CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 on October 12. CISA issued ICSA-25-140-03 in August 2025 covering both Danfoss and Copeland units.
- Pentest Partners notes separately that in unrelated research, now in coordinated disclosure, they found internet-exposed refrigeration controllers from another vendor already implanted by a botnet. The implant was pulled and analyzed. Device constraints rule out crypto mining and DDoS; the assessment is that the campaign is collecting persistent access footholds on the same class of device. Details will follow once disclosure completes.
Practitioner takeaway: If you support or investigate OT environments with refrigeration or building controllers, start by establishing whether contractor remote access runs through a managed, documented connection or a contractor-owned cellular modem the asset owner cannot see. That blind spot is how these units ended up exposed. For incident response on Danfoss AK-SM units, the xml.cgi request path is the access vector to look for in any available logs. Check firmware versions against the 4.2 release that removed the date-code login. ICSA-25-140-03 and CERTFR-2026-ALE-012 are the authoritative advisories.

item.title: Volexity Uncovers Stealthy Ivanti VPN Attack Using Three Zero-Day Vulnerabilities
item.description:
Three chained zero-days in Ivanti Connect Secure gave UTA0576 unauthenticated root access on a fully patched appliance, enabling credential theft and AD reconnaissance before detection. CVE-2026-104935 is actively exploited and in CISA KEV.
- CVE-2026-104935 (CVSS 8.6) covers both the authentication bypass and the race-condition RCE, and it is actively exploited in the wild with a CISA KEV listing as of this week. The auth bypass abuses a mismatch in how welcome.cgi validates the request URL versus the HTTP header it actually routes to, allowing an unauthenticated request to reach protected internal scripts. The RCE follows immediately: a Perl script disguised as a ZIP file is uploaded through a separate endpoint, the server schedules deletion after the ZIP validation fails, and the attacker races multiple requests to the file's predictable disk location before it disappears. The third flaw, privilege escalation from the web server account to root via the dsinvoked background service, has no patch yet.
- The privilege escalation is the detail defenders need to understand. UTA0576 patched the dsinvoked service's shared configuration store in memory, redirected a legitimate scheduled task to the Perl interpreter, triggered it, got root execution, then silently restored the config. No permanent disk changes. That is why Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool saw nothing: it checks on-disk files only, making a clean ICT result meaningless as an indicator of compromise on appliances exposed before the October 13 patch.
- Post-exploitation went straight for high-value AD secrets. UTA0576 deployed a custom Python LDAP tool that authenticated to an internal domain controller using the VPN appliance's own service account and queried Active Directory specifically for LAPS local administrator passwords, BitLocker recovery keys, and any attributes containing plaintext passwords. Results were compressed, encoded, and exfiltrated back through the exploit channel. The attacker also ran a packet capture tool (renamed and hidden in a directory absent from normal file listings, using eight rotating capture files to overwrite older traffic) to harvest cleartext credentials from LDAP traffic on the device, built a custom Kerberos implementation to run Kerberoasting, and conducted password spraying against AD accounts.
- Forensic anti-detection was deliberate. UTA0576 deleted selected Ivanti debug log entries and Linux audit log entries covering the attack window. Temporary files were removed after use. Commands were re-executed by repeating the full exploit chain each time rather than leaving a persistent web shell or backdoor, and results came back over normal HTTPS responses. The earliest evidence of access is October 3; the investigation began October 5. That two-day gap with no persistent implant and memory-only config changes illustrates how little traditional IOC hunting would have surfaced.
Takeaway: a clean Integrity Checker result does not clear an ICS appliance. Scope your investigation to memory artifacts, LDAP authentication logs from your domain controllers (look for the VPN appliance's service account running unexpected AD attribute queries, particularly ms-Mcs-AdmPwd, BitLocker recovery key attributes, and userPassword), and Linux audit log gaps covering the October 3-5 window. Apply the October 13 patch immediately. The privilege escalation fix is still pending, so network-segment the appliance and treat its service account credentials as compromised until reissued.

Scope your investigation to memory artifacts, LDAP authentication logs from your domain controllers (look for the VPN appliance's service account running unexpected AD attribute queries, particularly ms-Mcs-AdmPwd, BitLocker recovery key attributes, and userPassword), and Linux audit log gaps covering the October 3-5 window. Apply the October 13 patch immediately. The privilege escalation fix is still pending, so network-segment the appliance and treat its service account credentials as compromised until reissued.

item.title: CVE-2026-104935: Ivanti Connect Secure Zero-Day Exploited for Unauthenticated Code Execution
item.description:
CVE-2026-104935 in Ivanti Connect Secure is a CVSS 8.6 zero-day actively exploited in the wild, enabling unauthenticated root-level code execution via a three-vulnerability chain. CISA added it to KEV on October 13 with a federal remediation deadline of October 16.
Key findings:
- The exploitation chain begins at the publicly accessible /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi endpoint. Attackers supply an X-DSCGI-PATH HTTP header pointing to a protected CGI resource, routing unauthenticated requests to wu.cgi, an upload handler. A malicious Perl script disguised with a .zip extension is uploaded, briefly written to /home/runtime/tmp/, and executed via parallel requests referencing the temp path through the same header before deletion completes. The result is code execution as the lower-privileged cgi-server account. The separate privilege escalation then abuses the dsinvoked service and DSCache configuration store, modifying an Ivanti library in memory and causing dsinvoked to run attacker-controlled Perl as root.
- Volexity investigated a device running Ivanti Connect Secure 22.8R2.4, Build 19097, considered fully patched when malicious activity began October 3, 2026. The threat actor, tracked as UTA0576, re-executed the full exploit chain repeatedly rather than installing a persistent web shell, returning output through the exploit's own HTTPS traffic. This keeps disk artifacts minimal and is specifically designed to evade Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool, which focuses on file changes rather than in-memory modifications.
- Post-exploitation focused on credential and Active Directory access: the attackers extracted credentials from the appliance, queried LDAP, searched for Windows LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys, performed password spraying, captured LDAP traffic, and used custom Python and Kerberos tooling to test credentials. Reconnaissance and credential files were staged temporarily under /tmp/ before exfiltration and removal. The attackers also cleared entries from Ivanti debug logs and Linux audit logs. Attribution is uncertain: Volexity assesses with low confidence that UTA0576's motive may be criminal rather than espionage, and with medium confidence that the actor may have used large language models to assist exploit development.
- The privilege-escalation component used in the observed chain had no patch available as of October 13. Patching CVE-2026-104935 (which fixes the authentication bypass and RCE) is still the critical priority because blocking initial access prevents the escalation stage from being reached at all. Fixed releases are 22.8R2.5, 25.1.1.2, 25.1.3.0, and 25.1.3.1 depending on branch; Ivanti recommends migrating to the 25.x line as 22.x approaches end of life.
DFIR takeaway: Because disk artifacts are deliberately minimized, do not stop at the Integrity Checker. Hunt HTTP telemetry for requests to /dana-na/auth/url_default/welcome.cgi where X-DSCGI-PATH references wu.cgi or paths under /home/runtime/tmp/. Inspect /tmp/ for unexplained scripts. Look for unexpected outbound connections from the VPN appliance toward Active Directory, LDAP, DNS, or internal authentication systems, and investigate LDAP query patterns for LAPS or BitLocker attribute access, password spraying, and anomalous Kerberos activity. The known attacker IP from the investigated incident is 108.165.147[.]64 and suspicious activity involved /data/.icscap/. Treat all credentials accessible through the appliance, including LDAP service accounts, as potentially compromised and rotate after containment. Memory and network forensics are essential where compromise is suspected.

item.title: Case of AgentTesla Malware Distribution Disguised as a Business Proposal Email
item.description:
AgentTesla delivered via a four-stage .NET loader chain that hides payloads inside bitmap pixel data, with the dropper disguised as a Chinese 🇨🇳 café management app to slip past casual inspection.
Key findings:
- The phishing lure arrives as "{Company Name} LIST[.]ZIP" pretending to be a business proposal review request. Inside is a .NET EXE whose assembly metadata describes a café operations program in Chinese 🇨🇳, complete with UI code mimicking a café management interface. The gap between "product list" email and a café app binary is a fast triage signal.
- Payload delivery is entirely bitmap-based. Stage one (ProjectCafe.Form1.InitializeComponent) reads RGB pixel values from a resource named Fee to reconstruct a .NET DLL loaded via Assembly.Load. Stage two, disguised with Kingsoft security software metadata, reads the top-left 471x471 pixels of a resource named HATA, converts pixel data to a byte array, and XOR-decrypts it using a key derived from a value named yjw, then loads the result via AppDomain.Load. Stage three, labeled "Microsoft PC Manager" / "Microsoft Corporation," decrypts a resource named 8VXmw2w using byte operations keyed on the UTF-8 string ZIyStAzSE and drops the final payload.
- Persistence is lightweight but intentional: the stage-three loader copies the original running file to %APPDATA%\AH.Exe at startup. If AH.Exe already exists the copy is skipped, meaning this file on disk is the loader, not AgentTesla itself. Hunting for AH.Exe in %APPDATA% is a concrete pivot point.
- The final payload is AgentTesla, harvesting credentials, cookies, and contact data from browsers, email clients, FTP clients, and VPN software. Exfiltration goes out over FTP to server356.Web-hosting[.]Com using the account BBL[@]anmarinee[.]It[.]Com. The malware also queries the host's public IP and checks whether it is running inside a hosting environment before proceeding.
Responder action: hunt %APPDATA% for AH.Exe and trace its parent process chain back to the original ZIP-launched EXE. For network detection, watch for outbound FTP connections (port 21) to server356.Web-hosting[.]Com and the credential BBL[@]anmarinee[.]It[.]Com in any captured FTP authentication traffic. Any recovered browser credential stores, email client profiles (Outlook, Thunderbird), and FTP client configs should be treated as compromised and rotated. The multi-stage bitmap steganography means static AV on the EXE alone may not catch all stages; memory acquisition on a suspected host is the reliable path to recovering the intermediate DLLs.

item.title: Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver: How EDR Killing Became an Industry
item.description:
BYOVD EDR killing has industrialized into a tiered marketplace: ransomware crews disabled security tools in 48% of 2024 intrusions, and the kernel-level technique behind that number now ships as a versioned, affiliate-ready product with a price ladder and development pipeline.
Key details:
- The market has a documented price ladder and adoption chain. SentinelLABS tracked "Spyboy" selling the Terminator killer in 2023 at $300 to $3,000, then attributed AvNeutralizer (also known as AuKill) to FIN7, priced at $4,000 to $15,000 on Russian-language forums and abusing a Time Travel Debugging driver and the Process Explorer driver. That single tool spread into Black Basta, AvosLocker, MedusaLocker, BlackCat, Trigona, and LockBit operations. EDRKillShifter, first seen in a RansomHub attack in August 2024, abused RentDrv2 and ThreatFireMonitor drivers and extended to higher-tier affiliates. Gentlemen RaaS shipped a framework running eight-plus BYOVD variants targeting over 400 processes across 48 security products via DeviceIoControl calls, bundling third-party killers HexKiller and ThrottleBlood with a reported 90% affiliate revenue cut.
- CVE-anchored cases confirm the shared-driver-as-infrastructure model. DeadLock ransomware abused the Baidu driver BdApiUtil (CVE-2024-51324) to kill EDR and Windows Defender in December 2025. Reynolds ransomware embedded the NSecsoft driver NSecKrnl (CVE-2025-68947) to terminate more than 30 security processes in February 2026. The same NSecKrnl driver appears in Warlock operations, and Qilin chained rwdrv.sys with hlpdrv.sys in April 2026. Pivoting on driver hash groups campaigns by supplier across rival gangs.
- The kill chain is a fixed observable sequence with specific event IDs. Driver install via sc.exe surfaces as Sysmon Event ID 1 (process create) and System Event ID 7045 (service install). Driver load surfaces as Sysmon Event ID 6. The killer then issues DeviceIoControl calls, removes kernel callbacks, and terminates security processes. SOC Prime documented Qilin using hlpdrv.sys to strip registered kernel callbacks across more than 300 products: the sensor process stays running and reports healthy, so hunting only for killed processes misses this entirely. System Event ID 7031 (service crash) is rare in healthy environments and fires when the killer abruptly terminates a security service, making it a high-fidelity, low-false-positive alert candidate.
- Two driverless variants break the driver-load observable. EDR-Freeze exploits a Windows error-reporting race condition entirely in user mode. EDRSilencer blocks sensor telemetry using Windows filtering platform rules without touching a driver. Detections built only around driver loads miss both. Alert on the absence of signal: a lost heartbeat, an agent health drop, or a gap in a constant telemetry feed all read as tamper. Network, identity, and cloud telemetry remain available after the endpoint sensor is silenced and represent the residual investigation surface.
Practitioner takeaway: Hunt driver loads where the signature status is anything other than Valid, and alert on any driver whose hash, signer, or version has never appeared on that host before. Correlate Event ID 7045 (service install) plus Event ID 6 (driver load) in close sequence with a subsequent gap in EDR heartbeat or a 7031 service crash. The repeating rekill cadence, a kernel service polling the process list and issuing termination IOCTLs on a fixed interval, is itself a behavioral signal no legitimate service produces. IOCs and detection references for specific drivers (rwdrv.sys, hlpdrv.sys, NSecKrnl, RentDrv2, ThreatFireMonitor) are named in the report; the live LOLDrivers catalogue at loldrivers[.]io provides the broader driver inventory for blocklist comparison.

item.title: AhsayCBS Deep-Dive: Auth Bypass to RCE
item.description:
CVE-2026-105133 and CVE-2026-105134 in AhsayCBS are chained in the wild to drop webshells and execute commands as SYSTEM or root on backup servers. Hotfixes released 12 October 2026, weeks after active exploitation began.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-105133 is a trivially exploitable auth bypass in the JSONApi base class shared by every /rps/api/json/.do endpoint. A single JSON field, "FromServlet":"Y", sets a boolean that short-circuits the entire credential check. No session, no password, no valid account needed. From there, the unauthenticated caller hits AddSysUser to mint a local administrator with a login, password, and Role of their choosing, all from a single unauthenticated POST.
- CVE-2026-105134 is a path traversal write in the Replication Receiver's FileService at /rps/obs7/rpsfile. The attacker creates a receiver (auth-bypassed via the first CVE), controls its SystemHome, login, and password, then uses attacker-controlled X-RSW-Request-* headers (UserHome and TopDir) to build the write path. The path-building code in getReplicatedPath() strips % and : but leaves ../ untouched, and the denylist that blocks webapps/, conf/, and tomcat/ at receiver creation time is never consulted again at upload time. A UserHome of ../../webapps/rps walks directly into the live Tomcat application root.
- The result is a JSP webshell written under webapps/rps with a plain octet-stream PUT. Requesting /rps/status.jsp (or whichever filename the attacker chose) executes it. On Windows the AhsayCBS service runs as LocalSystem, so execution is SYSTEM. On Linux it runs as root. The same cbs.jar drives both platforms; the traversal logic accepts C:\... absolute paths and rewrites forward slashes to backslashes on Windows automatically.
- The full exploit chain is four steps: bypass auth, create a receiver with a controlled credential set, traverse into the web root, PUT the webshell. Horizon3[.]ai's proof of concept, including webshell cleanup, is published to their GitHub.
- The application is a Java/Tomcat stack installed from cbs-nix-tar.gz (Linux) or a Windows installer. Webapps of interest are webapps/rps (Replication Receiver), webapps/cbs (main console), and webapps/obs (backup client service). Routes are defined in webapps/rps/WEB-INF/struts-config.xml.
Responder takeaway: Start in the filesystem. Hunt for .jsp files under webapps/rps, webapps/cbs, or any served application directory, particularly files with recent mtime that are not part of the original install. On Windows, look for cbssvcX64.exe spawning cmd.exe, powershell.exe, curl, or certutil. On Linux, watch for the CBS JVM process forking shells or network tooling. In application logs, flag any "Logon to API from IP address" entry for accounts you did not provision, and pull ListSystemUsers to check for rogue admins. In access logs, requests to /rps/api/json/*.do carrying a FromServlet field or uploads to /rps/obs7/rpsfile with X-RSW-Request-* headers from external sources are the exploitation fingerprint. IOCs from observed attacks are in Huntress's report; the Horizon3[.]ai PoC is on their GitHub.

item.title: From One Account to Every Mailbox: Breaking Zimbra's Identity Boundaries (Part 1)
item.description:
Rapid7 discloses five chained Zimbra Collaboration Suite flaws enabling credential brute-force, full mailbox reading, SPF/DKIM-passing email impersonation, and silent mail exfiltration. Part 1 of a multi-part series covering 80+ vulnerabilities total.
Key findings:
- CVE-2026-93637 (CVSS 3.7) lets an unauthenticated attacker brute-force passwords through Zimbra's GraphQL endpoint at /service/extension/graphql without triggering the source-IP suspension counter. The ZimbraInvalidLoginFilter only increments its counter when the SOAP engine sets the auth.failed request attribute, but GraphQL calls the authentication handler directly via XMLDocumentUtilities.executeDocumentAsGuest(), bypassing SoapEngine entirely. GraphQL aliases allow batching of multiple password attempts in a single HTTP request: Rapid7 tested 10,000 candidates in under two minutes using 100 aliases per request. A Metasploit module ships with the PoC. When combined with CVE-2026-93635 (CVSS 5.3, an LDAP filter injection allowing wildcard username matching in external-LDAP configurations), per-account lockout also fails because the wildcarded login does not resolve to an existing local account. Neither CVE has a public fix at time of publication.
- CVE-2026-73571 (CVSS 8.3, fixed in ZCS 10.1.17) is an authorization failure in SaveDraftRequest. An authenticated user sets isDelegatedReq="1" and places any local address in the From field. The handler at SaveDraft.handle() resolves that address to its mailbox at [0] and constructs the OperationContext from it at [2] with no checkRight(), canAccessAccount(), or canSendAs() call before calling SendMsg.doSendMessage() at [3]. Because Zimbra submits the message through its own outbound pipeline, the result passes SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. A copy also lands in the impersonated user's Sent folder, creating a fabricated authorship record.
- CVE-2026-10631 (CVSS 6.5, fixed in ZCS 10.1.20) is an IDOR in the EWS extension. Zimbra's composite folder ID format encodes an owner UUID and numeric folder ID. FindItem passes the attacker-supplied UUID to ItemUtil.getGrantorMailbox(), which retrieves the victim mailbox without checking the caller. ItemOperation then builds an OperationContext from the victim mailbox at [4], the victim account becomes the authuser at [6], and Mailbox.getAuthenticatedAccount() at [7] treats the matching identity as owner access. Requires zimbraFeatureEwsEnabled=TRUE on the attacker account. The attacker obtains the victim's UUID via GetAccountInfoRequest or SearchGalRequest, then constructs IDs like {uuid}_2 (Inbox), {uuid}_5 (Sent), {uuid}_6 (Drafts), {uuid}_7 (Contacts), {uuid}_10 (Calendar). Works across servers in a cluster.
- CVE-2026-50055 (CVSS 6.5, fixed in ZCS 10.1.20) bypasses zimbraFeatureMailForwardingInFiltersEnabled=FALSE. The policy check in DocumentHandler.checkForwardFilterAttr() tests only for RedirectAction at [0], leaving NotifyAction and RFCCompliantNotifyAction unblocked. A Sieve actionNotify rule using ${subject}, ${from}, ${to}, and ${body} variables exfiltrates decoded headers and the full text body of every incoming message to an external address. The rule persists after the session expires or the password changes. In Zimbra Modern, the Filters view returns empty even while the server executes the active rule; Classic shows the rule name but not the external destination. Upgrading does not purge existing saved rules.
- DFIR response scope here is wider than a password reset. EWS access leaves no delegation grant to revoke. Sieve notify rules survive as saved account state in incoming and outgoing filter tables. Impersonation generates Sent folder artifacts and MTA relay records. Rapid7's report specifies that Modern's Filters view is insufficient for reviewing saved rules: administrators must inspect stored incoming and outgoing filter rules directly for external actionNotify and RFCCompliantNotifyAction entries. EWS logs expose cross-user operations involving two distinct account UUIDs. A reverse proxy inspecting request bodies can flag multiple authenticate aliases in a single anonymous GraphQL request to /service/extension/graphql. Full PoCs and per-CVE tracker entries are in Rapid7's accompanying GitHub repository. Parts 2 through 4 cover stored XSS, SSRF to code execution as zimbra, and zimbra-to-root paths.

item.content:encoded:
Rapid7 discloses five chained Zimbra Collaboration Suite flaws enabling credential brute-force, full mailbox reading, SPF/DKIM-passing email impersonation, and silent mail exfiltration. Part 1 of a multi-part series covering 80+ vulnerabilities total.

Key findings:

- CVE-2026-93637 (CVSS 3.7) lets an unauthenticated attacker brute-force passwords through Zimbra's GraphQL endpoint at /service/extension/graphql without triggering the source-IP suspension counter. The ZimbraInvalidLoginFilter only increments its counter when the SOAP engine sets the auth.failed request attribute, but GraphQL calls the authentication handler directly via XMLDocumentUtilities.executeDocumentAsGuest(), bypassing SoapEngine entirely. GraphQL aliases allow batching of multiple password attempts in a single HTTP request: Rapid7 tested 10,000 candidates in under two minutes using 100 aliases per request. A Metasploit module ships with the PoC. When combined with CVE-2026-93635 (CVSS 5.3, an LDAP filter injection allowing wildcard username matching in external-LDAP configurations), per-account lockout also fails because the wildcarded login does not resolve to an existing local account. Neither CVE has a public fix at time of publication.

- CVE-2026-73571 (CVSS 8.3, fixed in ZCS 10.1.17) is an authorization failure in SaveDraftRequest. An authenticated user sets isDelegatedReq="1" and places any local address in the From field. The handler at SaveDraft.handle() resolves that address to its mailbox at [0] and constructs the OperationContext from it at [2] with no checkRight(), canAccessAccount(), or canSendAs() call before calling SendMsg.doSendMessage() at [3]. Because Zimbra submits the message through its own outbound pipeline, the result passes SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. A copy also lands in the impersonated user's Sent folder, creating a fabricated authorship record.

- CVE-2026-10631 (CVSS 6.5, fixed in ZCS 10.1.20) is an IDOR in the EWS extension. Zimbra's composite folder ID format encodes an owner UUID and numeric folder ID. FindItem passes the attacker-supplied UUID to ItemUtil.getGrantorMailbox(), which retrieves the victim mailbox without checking the caller. ItemOperation then builds an OperationContext from the victim mailbox at [4], the victim account becomes the authuser at [6], and Mailbox.getAuthenticatedAccount() at [7] treats the matching identity as owner access. Requires zimbraFeatureEwsEnabled=TRUE on the attacker account. The attacker obtains the victim's UUID via GetAccountInfoRequest or SearchGalRequest, then constructs IDs like {uuid}_2 (Inbox), {uuid}_5 (Sent), {uuid}_6 (Drafts), {uuid}_7 (Contacts), {uuid}_10 (Calendar). Works across servers in a cluster.

- CVE-2026-50055 (CVSS 6.5, fixed in ZCS 10.1.20) bypasses zimbraFeatureMailForwardingInFiltersEnabled=FALSE. The policy check in DocumentHandler.checkForwardFilterAttr() tests only for RedirectAction at [0], leaving NotifyAction and RFCCompliantNotifyAction unblocked. A Sieve actionNotify rule using ${subject}, ${from}, ${to}, and ${body} variables exfiltrates decoded headers and the full text body of every incoming message to an external address. The rule persists after the session expires or the password changes. In Zimbra Modern, the Filters view returns empty even while the server executes the active rule; Classic shows the rule name but not the external destination. Upgrading does not purge existing saved rules.

- DFIR response scope here is wider than a password reset. EWS access leaves no delegation grant to revoke. Sieve notify rules survive as saved account state in incoming and outgoing filter tables. Impersonation generates Sent folder artifacts and MTA relay records. Rapid7's report specifies that Modern's Filters view is insufficient for reviewing saved rules: administrators must inspect stored incoming and outgoing filter rules directly for external actionNotify and RFCCompliantNotifyAction entries. EWS logs expose cross-user operations involving two distinct account UUIDs. A reverse proxy inspecting request bodies can flag multiple authenticate aliases in a single anonymous GraphQL request to /service/extension/graphql. Full PoCs and per-CVE tracker entries are in Rapid7's accompanying GitHub repository. Parts 2 through 4 cover stored XSS, SSRF to code execution as zimbra, and zimbra-to-root paths.

item.title: Iron Man & YamStore: Powering a Global Phishing-as-a-Service Ecosystem
item.description:
Chinese 🇨🇳 operators behind "Iron Man System" PhaaS ran 2,360 phishing templates across 130 countries, targeting over 75,000 organizations. Microsoft's DCU led a disruption of the core infrastructure in coordination with Resecurity.
Key findings:
- Iron Man System is a containerized, subscription-licensed phishing kit distributed via a self-hosted Gitea instance at docker.aidchildren[.]cc and docker.loveboy[.]xyz. Version 6.3.1 ships a bilingual Chinese 🇨🇳/English admin panel, a guided installer console at install.loveboy[.]xyz, and a build pipeline that published 911 container image versions, with the most recent pushed within days of this report. The kit is designed for non-technical buyers, turnkey deployment, and requires no coding skill to operate, which is why scale reaches 75,000 organizations and an estimated 1 billion phishing emails sent.
- Every active deployment phones home to api2.peaceman[.]cc for license authorization approximately every 20 seconds. Auxiliary endpoints ipapi2.peaceman[.]cc and bin2.peaceman[.]cc were observed alongside the primary host; log2.peaceloving[.]xyz handles telemetry beaconing on a recurring timer. Captured victim data and product-catalog images are stored at ossapi.haoeryu[.]top, an S3-compatible MinIO-pattern backend fronted by a CDN/reverse-proxy. Static credentials were found shipped across multiple historical container builds, not unique per deployment.
- The template catalog, snapshotted through 1 October 2026, covers 551 distinct lure-type tags. Top impersonated brands include dhl[.]com (37 templates), dpd[.]com (24), apple[.]com (23), gls-group[.]com (22), americanexpress[.]com (12), and amazon[.]com (12). Courier and postal impersonation is the largest single category, consistent with high-volume smishing rather than targeted BEC. Catalog growth peaked at 322 templates added in May 2026 and remained elevated through the reporting period, 17.4 GB of lure bundles downloaded across 1,566 cataloged entries.
- The build registry's public user directory exposed eight operator accounts without authentication, with registration dates from October 2025 through June 2026. The admin account uses the email domain aidchildren, matching one of the kit's own hostnames, consistent with it being the core developer account. Remaining accounts use QQ, Gmail, and ProtonMail addresses. The internal binary ships a controller at the package path devops-super/internal/controller/remotegoods and captures victim submission records containing SelectGoods, goods_name, goods_price alongside card_number, expiry_date, and verify_code, meaning this kit harvests full payment card data paired with purchase-item context, not just credentials.
Practitioner takeaway: the licensing dependency is your highest-value disruption and detection point. Every active Iron Man deployment polls api2.peaceman[.]cc every 20 seconds. Block or sinkhole that domain and the panel degrades across all buyer deployments simultaneously. For hunting, look for outbound DNS and HTTPS to the peaceman[.]cc, peaceloving[.]xyz, haoeryu[.]top, aidchildren[.]cc, and loveboy[.]xyz domain families in proxy and DNS logs. Container environments pulling images from docker.aidchildren[.]cc or docker.loveboy[.]xyz warrant immediate triage. The full IOC table is in the Resecurity report.

item.title: Break the silence: Kazakhstan-nexus UAT-6275 targets CIS government organizations
item.description:
Kazakhstan-nexus UAT-6275 targets CIS governments with four distinct infection chains, custom reverse shells, and a WinRAR CVE-2025-8088 exploit, active June 2025 through August 2026.
Key findings:
- UAT-6275 (also tracked as TAG-193 by Recorded Future, and overlapping with Silent Lynx, YoroTrooper, Tomiris, ShadowSilk, Cavalry Werewolf, and Hydra Saiga) ran at least eight campaigns across nine countries: Kazakhstan 🇰🇿, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Russia 🇷🇺, and Belarus 🇧🇾. Targets include diplomatic, agriculture, environmental, and energy ministries. Network flow analysis tied intrusion activity to specific treaty discussions and bilateral meetings in early 2026, suggesting the group pursues timely intelligence on regional negotiations.
- Four infection chains evolved over the observation window. Chain A (June 2025): macro-enabled Word documents download and execute a second-stage binary. Chain B (July 2025): PS2EXE-packaged PowerShell downloaders retrieve reverse shells and create scheduled tasks for persistence. Chain C (October 2025): malicious shortcuts launch PowerShell to pull GitHub-hosted scripts, with later samples also dropping PickleShell into the Windows Startup folder. Chain D (April 2026): a crafted RAR archive exploits CVE-2025-8088 in WinRAR to write PickleShell directly to the Startup folder, executing at next user sign-in. This is the first vulnerability exploit observed in UAT-6275 delivery.
- Three custom reverse shells anchor the post-compromise toolkit: Chvost, Laplas, and PickleShell. Recovered infrastructure also contained Linux-compatible tooling and a publicly available proof-of-concept exploit for FortiWeb CVE-2025-25257, indicating the group is preparing to expand operations beyond Windows endpoints to Linux hosts and internet-facing appliances.
- Three exposed staging directories and a previously unreported GitHub repository gave Talos direct visibility into payload builds, tool inventories, and C2 changes through commit history. Timing of 77 GitHub commits clusters within UTC+5 working hours (09:00-18:00 local), and malware-testing submissions from Kazakhstan 🇰🇿 shortly after compilation support a medium-confidence Kazakhstan 🇰🇿 nexus assessment.
- ClamAV signatures are available: Win.Backdoor.PickleShell-10060602-0, Win.Backdoor.Chvost-10060603-0, Win.Malware.LAPLAS-10060605-0, Win.Malware.LAPLAS-10060606-0, Win.Proxy.Generic-10060628-0. Snort 2 rules 1:11192, 1:15306, 1:46983, 1:47398 and Snort 3 rules 1:46983, 4:16 also cover this threat.
For defenders in CIS government, energy, and environmental sectors: hunt for PowerShell spawning from shortcut (LNK) files, unexpected scheduled task creation, and new entries in the Windows Startup folder, particularly PickleShell drops. Verify WinRAR is patched against CVE-2025-8088 and audit any RAR extraction that places executables outside the destination directory. IOCs are in the Cisco Talos GitHub repository linked in the Virus Bulletin white paper "Break the Silence: Tracking Silent Lynx Through Exposed Infrastructure."

item.title: The eBPF forensics gap and what your EDR cannot see
item.description:
eBPF rootkits and Linux EDR share the same kernel privilege level, meaning your sensor and the implant read the same data structures, and only one of them decides what the other sees.
Key findings:
- LinkPro and VoidLink demonstrate how far this tradecraft has matured. LinkPro intercepts sys_bpf so its programs vanish from bpftool prog list. VoidLink fires a kernel timer every five seconds scanning for process names like bpftool, bpftrace, strace, gdb, and perf, pausing or self-destructing when it finds them. Its ss-hiding technique uses bpf_probe_write_user to lengthen the previous netlink message so hidden socket entries are swallowed as padding and never parsed. Running bpftool on a suspect host is itself a knock on the door. VoidLink was reportedly built by a single developer in under a week with AI-assisted development, suggesting the cost of this tradecraft is falling faster than the cost of the tools hunting it.
- The live system is the weakest witness available. Rootkits that intercept bpf_ringbuf_submit drop telemetry records before user-space ever sees them: the dashboard stays green, the activity never happened. io_uring lets a process batch file, network, and process operations into a handful of syscalls, leaving per-syscall sensors blind to a significant slice of activity. Cross-view checks like comparing ss output against /proc/net/tcp can catch VoidLink when its hide lists drift out of sync, but when both views agree they prove very little.
- A memory image bypasses the syscall interface a rootkit filters. Volatility 3's mainline linux.ebpf plugin walks the kernel's prog_idr and returns name, tag, and type for each loaded program. Community plugins from the 2023 Volatility contest add helper-based scoring, JIT code dumping, map enumeration, and attachment graphs. VoidLink's hidden_ports map, sitting in memory, lists exactly what the operator wanted concealed, including port 8080 by default. VoidLink also pairs its eBPF component with a kernel module that unlinks itself from the module list and masquerades as the AMD memory encryption driver, so linux.modxview and linux.netfilter matter alongside linux.ebpf. The ICMP command channel rides on Netfilter hooks, which linux.netfilter surfaces.
- Auditd record type 1334, introduced via a Daniel Borkmann patch in 2019, captures every eBPF program load and unload on x86_64 hosts when enabled with: auditctl -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S bpf. It records who loaded which program number and when, not what the program does. Elastic ships a detection rule correlating bpf_probe_write_user and bpf_override_return with load paths like world-writable directories. The kernel also logs a warning when bpf_probe_write_user is installed. VoidLink waits three seconds after its kernel module loads before installing hooks, long enough to outlast a synchronous check of the new module.
- Kernel lockdown, recommended by Elastic against this class of malware and available since Linux 5.4, blocks AVML from reading /proc/kcore, /dev/mem, or /dev/crash. Hardening that blocks your own forensics is a debt paid at the worst moment. The acquisition path must be decided before the incident: a signed LiME module prepared per kernel build, or acquisition from the hypervisor layer to keep the rootkit away from the acquisition process entirely.
Practitioner takeaway: Do not reboot before capturing memory. eBPF implants live in kernel memory and disappear with it. Build your baseline now on known-good hosts using bpftool prog list and bpftool map list, and keep Volatility symbol tables for every kernel in your fleet because the mainline plugin fails without prog_idr. On the analysis workstation, run linux.ebpf, linux.modxview, linux.netfilter, and linux.psscan against the image, then query the load timeline with ausearch -m 1334 --start today. The report includes detection logic and acquisition command examples.

item.title: From ClickFix to C2: Comparative Analysis of Two Malware Loaders
item.description:
ClickFix-delivered Lorem Ipsum Loader and Axolotl share C2 infrastructure and registration protocol, with Vice Society-linked tradecraft targeting ransomware deployment via a custom Python TCP tunnel implant.
Key findings:
- Lorem Ipsum Loader arrives via DLL sideloading inside a ZIP (vdsldr.exe/vdsutil.dll or CertEnrollCtrl.exe/CertEnroll.dll plus 1.bat), which writes an HKCU Run key and a scheduled task both named with the pattern basename_<9 random chars>, running /sc minute /mo 60. The DLL carries a non-standard .cpoc section encoding the payload as NULL-separated five-letter words indexed against an RT_RCDATA dictionary. Forescout also confirmed a previously unreported staged delivery: a trojanized MT_setup_v3.22.7182.msi (SHA256 13a3fa500e91e35a34f71e0e88f07a5b3dd8251e9b423188030e31dbd8eaf603) drops stage_03_aes_decrypted.ps1, which GZIP-decompresses and executes o1.ps1 in memory. Attributed to Rapid Brigantine, a.k.a. Vanilla Tempest / Vice Society, which has deployed Rhysida, BlackCat, and Quantum Locker.
- The C2 registration sequence is shared between both loader families and is a high-confidence detection point: a POST to /api/init/<uuid> with Content-Type: image/jpeg, a roughly 10 KB decoy JPEG body, and User-Agent Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:143.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/143.0, sent via WinHTTP. The C2 domain list is retrieved first via a dead-drop profile on letsdiskuss[.]com/user/lindawilliams51453 (also dhuahsd12d2752 and joeblack1673), with the domain list framed by -=( and )=- markers. Confirmed Lorem Ipsum C2 hosts: scriptedgeapp[.]com (213.109.203[.]107), transferrootway[.]com (45.66.249[.]57), updaterdeskarc[.]com (185.28.119[.]81), and signinbyte[.]com (185.28.119[.]14), all on AS62005 / BlueVPS OU. Axolotl shares the same ASN via bloganimals[.]com (185.28.119[.]138). The 185.28.119.0/24 range is a reliable pivot for retrohunting.
- The final payload is client[.]py, a custom Python TCP tunnel that connects to the C2 over TLS on port 443, upgrades to WebSocket at /tunnel, and sends the per-sample UUID as MSG_HANDSHAKE (0x07). The server then opens arbitrary TCP streams through the implant using MSG_CONNECT (0x01), enabling full lateral movement capability. The WebSocket-over-TLS transport with browser-like headers is deliberately designed to blend with normal HTTPS traffic. The incident Forescout investigated was contained before ransomware deployed, but client[.]py was the pivot point intended to enable it.
- Axolotl Loader breaks into three variants (A1, A2, B) across 39 samples, all signed by "BUSINESS CONSULTING SP Z O O" (serial 330007dc4e73fc0b983770783900000007dc4e, validity 2026-02-19 to 2026-02-22, issuer Microsoft ID Verified CS AOC CA 01). Variant B abuses ieinstal.exe and the IActiveXInstallBroker CLSID {BDB57FF2-79B9-4205-9447-F5FE85F37312} to redirect HKLM/HKCR to HKCU via RegOverridePredefKey and can write ICDRegOCX RunOnce values calling rundll32.exe IEAdvpack.dll RegisterOCX. All 39 decrypted shellcodes carry a 0x6997XXXX stack-junk pattern absent from Lorem Ipsum. Lorem Ipsum DLLs are unsigned and use WinHTTP rather than Axolotl's WinINet, add ntdll unhooking and process injection, and resolve C2 dynamically rather than hardcoding it.
Practitioners: Hunt Sysmon Event 7 for vdsldr.exe or CertEnrollCtrl.exe loading a paired DLL from outside System32 or WinSxS. Correlate Sysmon Event 13 on HKCU\...\CurrentVersion\Run with TaskScheduler/Operational Event 106 for the same basename_<9chars> name within the same minute. Review proxy and DNS logs for non-browser processes resolving letsdiskuss[.]com or digitalpoint[.]com, and search those platforms' profile pages for the -=( and )=- pattern to identify active dead drops. Alert on any PE signed by "BUSINESS CONSULTING SP Z O O" or serial 330007dc. Flag POST /api/init/ with Content-Type: image/jpeg from non-browser processes. Full IOC table and TTPs are in the Forescout report.

Forescout also confirmed a previously unreported staged delivery: a trojanized MT_setup_v3.22.7182.msi (SHA256 13a3fa500e91e35a34f71e0e88f07a5b3dd8251e9b423188030e31dbd8eaf603) drops stage_03_aes_decrypted.ps1, which GZIP-decompresses and executes o1.ps1 in memory. Attributed to Rapid Brigantine, a.k.a. Vanilla Tempest / Vice Society, which has deployed Rhysida, BlackCat, and Quantum Locker.

- The C2 registration sequence is shared between both loader families and is a high-confidence detection point: a POST to /api/init/<uuid> with Content-Type: image/jpeg, a roughly 10 KB decoy JPEG body, and User-Agent Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:143.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/143.0, sent via WinHTTP. The C2 domain list is retrieved first via a dead-drop profile on letsdiskuss[.]com/user/lindawilliams51453 (also dhuahsd12d2752 and joeblack1673), with the domain list framed by -=( and )=- markers. Confirmed Lorem Ipsum C2 hosts: scriptedgeapp[.]com (213.109.203[.]107), transferrootway[.]com (45.66.249[.]57), updaterdeskarc[.]com (185.28.119[.]81), and signinbyte[.]com (185.28.119[.]14), all on AS62005 / BlueVPS OU. Axolotl shares the same ASN via bloganimals[.]com (185.28.119[.]138). The 185.28.119.0/24 range is a reliable pivot for retrohunting.

- The final payload is client[.]py, a custom Python TCP tunnel that connects to the C2 over TLS on port 443, upgrades to WebSocket at /tunnel, and sends the per-sample UUID as MSG_HANDSHAKE (0x07). The server then opens arbitrary TCP streams through the implant using MSG_CONNECT (0x01), enabling full lateral movement capability. The WebSocket-over-TLS transport with browser-like headers is deliberately designed to blend with normal HTTPS traffic. The incident Forescout investigated was contained before ransomware deployed, but client[.]py was the pivot point intended to enable it.

- Axolotl Loader breaks into three variants (A1, A2, B) across 39 samples, all signed by "BUSINESS CONSULTING SP Z O O" (serial 330007dc4e73fc0b983770783900000007dc4e, validity 2026-02-19 to 2026-02-22, issuer Microsoft ID Verified CS AOC CA 01). Variant B abuses ieinstal.exe and the IActiveXInstallBroker CLSID {BDB57FF2-79B9-4205-9447-F5FE85F37312} to redirect HKLM/HKCR to HKCU via RegOverridePredefKey and can write ICDRegOCX RunOnce values calling rundll32.exe IEAdvpack.dll RegisterOCX. All 39 decrypted shellcodes carry a 0x6997XXXX stack-junk pattern absent from Lorem Ipsum. Lorem Ipsum DLLs are unsigned and use WinHTTP rather than Axolotl's WinINet, add ntdll unhooking and process injection, and resolve C2 dynamically rather than hardcoding it.

Practitioners: Hunt Sysmon Event 7 for vdsldr.exe or CertEnrollCtrl.exe loading a paired DLL from outside System32 or WinSxS. Correlate Sysmon Event 13 on HKCU\...\CurrentVersion\Run with TaskScheduler/Operational Event 106 for the same basename_<9chars> name within the same minute. Review proxy and DNS logs for non-browser processes resolving letsdiskuss[.]com or digitalpoint[.]com, and search those platforms' profile pages for the -=( and )=- pattern to identify active dead drops. Alert on any PE signed by "BUSINESS CONSULTING SP Z O O" or serial 330007dc. Flag POST /api/init/ with Content-Type: image/jpeg from non-browser processes. Full IOC table and TTPs are in the Forescout report.

item.title: Fake AI Tools Put US Companies at Risk: Inside Counterfeit Claude, ChatGPT, and Copilot
item.description:
Fake AI tool campaigns impersonating Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, and Gemini delivered infostealers, RATs, and session-cookie stealers to US 🇺🇸 organizations across 1,258 sandbox analyses from April to October 2026, with developers and marketing teams as the primary targets.
Key findings:
- Claude and ChatGPT account for 81% of the activity: 601 analyses (48%) tied to Claude lures, 418 (33%) to ChatGPT and Codex. The US 🇺🇸 ranks first in both the fake "Download Claude" campaign (21 of 92 country records) and ChatGPT-themed chains (18 of 86), and second overall at 16% of 422 records. Industries appearing across the most campaign queries include technology, telecommunications, education, consulting, and manufacturing, sectors with large developer and knowledge-worker populations.
- Five distinct attack patterns drove the volume. InstallFix (341 analyses, T1204.004) swaps the vendor domain in a legitimate-looking one-liner so "irm claudecode[.]us[.]com/install.ps1 | iex" pulls from refract3[.]com then kafeprog7[.]com or help.xenngypt[.]com, ending in a stealer from a GitHub release. ClickFix (220 analyses, T1218.005) clones the Claude download page on cladesktop-apps[.]com, GitLab Pages, and Cloudflare Pages, uses mshta to fetch an HTA from last-version.install-2026[.]com, assembles "powershell" from string fragments to bypass matching, and delivers a stealer with no file ever touching the browser's download folder. A third pattern publishes the lure directly on claude[.]ai and chatgpt[.]com as shared artifacts or custom GPTs: a curl one-liner decodes a base64 URL pointing to paripassuventures[.]com to deliver MacSync Stealer on macOS, while a shared ChatGPT chat redirects to openai-backup[.]one for a ClickFix-style MSI drop.
- The trojanized installer pattern (T1053.005, T1539) is the most forensically rich. claude-ai[.]us delivers Claude_x64-setup.exe (SHA-256: 882b1aa5432509df9b1ac29b6f987a5dd70c8f46009237de956275a58536f470) from a GitHub release as a decoy while a stager registers the victim via /api4.php?method=auth and creates a scheduled task named mseupdate that launches msedge.exe headless with remote-debugging-port=9222 and user-agent "Google Update 4.3". Cookies, browser extensions, and keystrokes are then posted to nucleflowers[.]xyz via /api2.php?method=sendcookjson, sendexts, and sendkeys. Session access follows without any new MFA prompt.
- The AI Ads browser-in-the-browser (BiTB) pattern targets marketing staff with fake invitations to "Run ads on Claude" or connect Google Ads to Gemini (claude-advertisement[.]com, gemini-beta-invitations[.]com, perplexity-beta-ads[.]com, beta-manus[.]com). The fake Google sign-in window is drawn inside the page, with a live socket.io channel to the operator. Backend API paths are identical across all four brands: POST /api/create/user, POST /api/send/ip, GET /api/checkBan/, GET /api/checkDone/. These paths, not the rotating domains, are the stable hunting key.
- Separately named malware posing as AI apps added 220 analyses: fake claude-code.exe carrying Aura Stealer (SHA-256: e86f7ba0413a3a4b1d7e1a275b3d1ef62345c9d3fd761635ff188119b8122c85) with C2 at sys-tools[.]cfd, Copilot-named files carrying AsyncRAT (8 analyses), and grok.exe carrying Quasar RAT. T1583.008 (malvertising) and T1608.006 (SEO poisoning) drove initial access; confirmed MITRE IDs in the report also include T1059.001, T1059.004, T1218.005, T1218.007, and T1555.003.
Hunt for the behavioral residue that outlasted the domains: the mseupdate scheduled task running msedge.exe with --remote-debugging-port=9222 and user-agent "Google Update 4.3", mshta.exe spawning from a browser process, irm ... | iex one-liners where the domain is not a known vendor, and POST requests to /api2.php with sendcookjson, sendexts, or sendkeys in the path. The report lists the full IOC table, defanged domains, hashes, operator key, and MITRE mapping.
